newsitem.title: USA: Third wave of tobacco suits led to settlement.
newsitem.headline: Third wave of tobacco suits led to settlement.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

The unprecented number of attacks on the tobacco industry that led to Friday's historic settlement comprises the third wave of litigation aimed at proving cigarette companies hid the health risks of smoking.

This latest wave, which began in 1994, differs from the first two in that most cases focus on the addictive nature of nicotine and allegations that the tobacco industry manipulates the level of nicotine to keep smokers hooked.

The first two waves were from 1954 to 1973 and 1983 to 1992, according to lawyers who have tracked cases against the tobacco industry. The earlier personal injury cases against the industry failed as jurors repeatedly viewed smoking as a matter of choice and blamed individuals for their decision to start smoking and inability to stop.

Jury consultants believe that this attitude is changing due to internal tobacco documents, which have been surfacing since 1994, that critics say appear to indicate that the industry viewed cigarettes as nicotine delivery devices and purposely marketed the products to children.
There have only been two times in which a jury has awarded damages to a plaintiff.

The first was the landmark Cipollone case, which was the first tobacco case reviewed by the U.S. Supreme Court. In that case, a federal jury in Newark, N.J., in 1988 awarded $400,000 to the husband of Rose Cipollone, who died of lung cancer. She had smoked for 42 years and was 58 when she died in 1984, a year after the lawsuit was filed.

The second award was given by a Jacksonville, Fla., jury on Aug. 9, 1996. It awarded $750,000 to a man who smoked for 44 years before developing lung cancer. The jury said the Lucky Strikes he smoked were a defective product and that manufacturer Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. was negligent by failing to inform the public about health risks of smoking.

The earlier Cipollone case was argued twice before the Supreme Court and resulted in a June 24, 1992, landmark ruling that the federally mandated warning on cigarette packages did not protect tobacco companies from personal injury suits.

In its ruling, the nation's highest court overturned a finding by the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia that smokers could not sue cigarette companies for injuries that stemmed from their smoking after Jan. 1, 1966, when the warning law took effect.

The Supreme Court sent the Cipollone case back for retrial in New Jersey, but the lawsuit was dropped in 1992 when the law firm that had been representing the plaintiffs could no longer afford to fight the tobacco industry.

The same firm filed another significant tobacco lawsuit in 1984 on behalf of Susan Haines, who sued the industry over her father's death from lung cancer. The firm also withdrew from the Haines case but it is now being handled by the Charleston, S.C., firm of Ness, Motley, Loadholt, Richardson & Poole, which is active in other tobacco cases.

The Haines case, which is pending in a federal court in Newark, N.J., is important because certain internal tobacco documents obtained in its discovery stage resulted in a controversial public rebuke of the tobacco industry by the then-trial judge and led to at least one of the ongoing federal criminal probes.

In 1992, H. Lee Sarokin, who was a federal district judge then, reviewed the sealed documents and said "the tobacco industry may be the king of concealment and disinformation" and that the documents contained evidence of fraud.
Some of those documents also were among sensitive papers turned over by the Liggett Group as part of its March 1997 settlement with state attorneys general suing to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers.

Although the Supreme Court's ruling in Cipollone and Sarokin's revelations about the documents in Haines were expected to open the door to a flood of litigation against cigarette companies, the industry remained successful in fighting off lawsuits with its seemingly bottomless war chest.
The picture changed drastically in early 1994 with the wide publicity of internal tobacco documents concerning the industry's knowledge about nicotine and addiction.

Since that time, attacks on the industry have mounted rapidly with hundreds of individual and class-action lawsuits being filed across the country. One lawyer in Florida, for example, boasts of more than 1,000 clients.
The industry suffered a harsh blow in April 1997 when a federal judge upheld the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's authority to regulate cigarettes as a drug delivery device.

Another devastating attack came from the state Medicaid lawsuits. Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, the first of the attorneys general to file in 1994, encouraged a majority of his colleagues to join the battle. Moore has been a key negotiator in the historic settlement with the industry.

Even with the settlement of civil lawsuits, the industry still faces the threat of criminal action. The Justice Department continues its investigation into whether the tobacco companies and its executives have lied to Congress and federal agencies about the health risks of smoking.
